beats.narration_text: This is a Final Project Pitch Film created by Ethan Gomes. The project is called Data Sentry, and its first pieces already run. The question isn't whether Claude can write data checks. It's whether anyone can measure what they miss.

shot.visual_intent: Title card: 'DataSentry' large and centred; a thin rule draws beneath it with one terracotta dot; one line below: 'Scoring AI-written data checks with planted defects'.
shot.motion_claim: Title card: 'DataSentry' large and centred; a thin rule draws beneath it with one terracotta dot; one line below: 'Scoring AI-written data checks with planted defects'.

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell: one drawn object on a cream stage, a label or two; the voice explains. Only underfill and clustered are waived; edge-bleed, empty-frame and contrast still apply.

beats.narration_text: In plain words: companies set rules to catch bad data, like a taxi fare below zero. Data Sentry tests those rules the way you'd test a spell-checker: hide some mistakes on purpose, then count which ones it catches, and which slip through.

shot.visual_intent: Plain-language picture: a page of writing; terracotta marks are hidden in it on purpose; a magnifier passes over and ticks the ones it finds; one mark is left with no tick ('slipped through').
shot.motion_claim: Plain-language picture: a page of writing; terracotta marks are hidden in it on purpose; a magnifier passes over and ticks the ones it finds; one mark is left with no tick ('slipped through').

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell: one drawn object on a cream stage, a label or two; the voice explains. Only underfill and clustered are waived; edge-bleed, empty-frame and contrast still apply.

beats.narration_text: Data Sentry has an AI write data checks for a table, then scores those checks by planting defects they have to catch.

shot.visual_intent: A checkpoint scanner arch lands on the stage with its floor shadow; the name 'DataSentry' sits beside it; a parcel (the table) slides under the arch.
shot.motion_claim: A checkpoint scanner arch lands on the stage with its floor shadow; the name 'DataSentry' sits beside it; a parcel (the table) slides under the arch.

beats.narration_text: When it's done, it will be a public GitHub repo with three parts: a part that writes checks, a defect planter, and a scorecard of what was caught and what was missed. All three have already run.

shot.visual_intent: A kraft crate labelled 'public GitHub repo / when done' opens; three parts rise beside it one by one, a check page, a dark planter block, a binder; each labelled once.
shot.motion_claim: A kraft crate labelled 'public GitHub repo / when done' opens; three parts rise beside it one by one, a check page, a dark planter block, a binder; each labelled once.

beats.narration_text: It starts from public data. My first run used New York City yellow taxi trips from January twenty twenty-five, sampled to ten thousand rows.

shot.visual_intent: A flat table card lands; column blocks and grey rows fill in; labels 'NYC taxi · Jan 2025' and the real sample size from the first run.
shot.motion_claim: A flat table card lands; column blocks and grey rows fill in; labels 'NYC taxi · Jan 2025' and the real sample size from the first run.

beats.narration_text: Under the hood, part one. Python and pandas load the table. A planter script makes copies, breaks each one a different way, five ways in all, and writes an answer key that no check ever reads.

shot.visual_intent: Pipeline, part one (exists): a table card, an arrow to a dark planter block, an arrow to a broken copy with terracotta marks, and a locked answer key beside it; labels 'pandas', 'planter', 'answer key'.
shot.motion_claim: Pipeline, part one (exists): a table card, an arrow to a dark planter block, an arrow to a broken copy with terracotta marks, and a locked answer key beside it; labels 'pandas', 'planter', 'answer key'.

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell: one drawn object on a cream stage, a label or two; the voice explains. Only underfill and clustered are waived; edge-bleed, empty-frame and contrast still apply.

beats.narration_text: Part two. Claude, Opus five point five, saw only the column names and types, and wrote pandera checks under a prompt contract. Each check runs on the clean copy and every broken copy, and a scorer compares the flags with the answer key, one defect type at a time.

shot.visual_intent: Pipeline, part two, titled 'Part 2': a workstation (Claude) writes check pages; the checks run over the clean and broken copies; the scorer binder lands with a tick and a dot (caught / missed); labels 'Claude / Opus 5.5', 'pandera checks', 'scorer'.
shot.motion_claim: Pipeline, part two, titled 'Part 2': a workstation (Claude) writes check pages; the checks run over the clean and broken copies; the scorer binder lands with a tick and a dot (caught / missed); labels 'Claude / Opus 5.5', 'pandera checks', 'scorer'.

beats.narration_text: Why would anyone care? I ran one rule, fare can't be negative, in two tools data teams use. In D B T, it passed the clean copy and failed twenty-five rows of the broken one.

shot.visual_intent: Recorded output (typeset) of the real dbt run: dbt build with the not_negative test PASS on trips_clean and FAIL 25 on trips_broken; tagged 'recorded output · <date>'.
shot.motion_claim: Recorded output (typeset) of the real dbt run: dbt build with the not_negative test PASS on trips_clean and FAIL 25 on trips_broken; tagged 'recorded output · <date>'.

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell: one drawn object on a cream stage, a label or two; the voice explains. Only underfill and clustered are waived; edge-bleed, empty-frame and contrast still apply.

beats.narration_text: In Great Expectations, with the free G X Core, the same: pass, then twenty-five unexpected values. Its paid G X Cloud adds Expect A I, which suggests checks for you. I tested that same idea with Claude.

shot.visual_intent: Recorded output (typeset) of the real GX Core run: ExpectColumnValuesToBeBetween(fare_amount, min_value=0), PASS on clean, FAIL 25 unexpected on broken; 'ExpectAI (GX Cloud): not run'.
shot.motion_claim: Recorded output (typeset) of the real GX Core run: ExpectColumnValuesToBeBetween(fare_amount, min_value=0), PASS on clean, FAIL 25 unexpected on broken; 'ExpectAI (GX Cloud): not run'.

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell: one drawn object on a cream stage, a label or two; the voice explains. Only underfill and clustered are waived; edge-bleed, empty-frame and contrast still apply.

beats.narration_text: But I had planted twenty-five trips that end before they start. None of the three tools flagged them, because no rule asked. Data Sentry tells a data engineer which bad rows their checks let through.

shot.visual_intent: Recorded output (typeset): the three tools side by side (all PASS clean, FAIL 25 broken), then the answer key: negative fares 25/25 CAUGHT, drop-off before pick-up 0/25 MISSED.
shot.motion_claim: Recorded output (typeset): the three tools side by side (all PASS clean, FAIL 25 broken), then the answer key: negative fares 25/25 CAUGHT, drop-off before pick-up 0/25 MISSED.

beats.narration_text: Who opens it? A hiring manager for a data engineering role. One command shows each defect type, caught or missed. My one hand-written rule caught two of five. Claude's first checks caught all five, but rejected two hundred twenty good trips. Its revision fixed that, and missed every negative fare.

shot.visual_intent: Recorded output (typeset) of the scorecard from ./score_round.sh 1 and 2: hand-written 1 rule, clean PASS, 2 of 5; Claude round 1, 220 clean rows flagged, 5 of 5; round 2, 1 check crashes, 4 of 5; round 2 negative fares 0/25 MISSED; tagged "Claude Opus 5.5 · recorded output · <date>".
shot.motion_claim: Recorded output (typeset) of the scorecard from ./score_round.sh 1 and 2: hand-written 1 rule, clean PASS, 2 of 5; Claude round 1, 220 clean rows flagged, 5 of 5; round 2, 1 check crashes, 4 of 5; round 2 negative fares 0/25 MISSED; tagged "Claude Opus 5.5 · recorded output · <date>".

beats.narration_text: What does it prove? Four skills from this class, each with a run behind it: a prompt contract, a two-round loop, a clean-copy control, and a catch rate per defect. I test an AI's output instead of trusting it.

shot.visual_intent: An evidence binder; its cover opens; four record sheets fan out in a row with ink numerals 1 to 4, one per skill named.
shot.motion_claim: An evidence binder; its cover opens; four record sheets fan out in a row with ink numerals 1 to 4, one per skill named.

beats.narration_text: In scope: one table, five defect types, one scorecard. Out of scope, on purpose: orchestration, so no Airflow. The first pieces have run, and each run saves its scorecard with the date.

shot.visual_intent: An 'in scope' box fills (table, defects, scorecard); Airflow stays outside; a printed slip with a tick, labelled with the date the first piece ran.
shot.motion_claim: An 'in scope' box fills (table, defects, scorecard); Airflow stays outside; a printed slip with a tick, labelled with the date the first piece ran.

beats.narration_text: What could sink it? Checks that are too strict, or too loose, like Claude's two rounds. So the clean copy and the broken copies are both required, every time.

shot.visual_intent: A permission gate with its barrier raised; a broken parcel rides straight through; then the barrier comes down and the next broken parcel stops.
shot.motion_claim: A permission gate with its barrier raised; a broken parcel rides straight through; then the barrier comes down and the next broken parcel stops.

beats.narration_text: Why this project? In my Food Inspections Dataset Project, my checks let bad rows through, and I didn't know which ones until later. Data Sentry measures exactly that. It's a mix: pandera, D B T, Great Expectations, and prompting Claude are new to me. Working with messy public data, I've done before, in that project.

shot.visual_intent: A table card labelled 'Food Inspections Dataset Project' gets terracotta marks (bad rows that got through); an arrow leads to two lists: 'New to me: pandera, dbt, GX, Claude' and 'Done before: messy public data'.
